title: Praise and blame
note: Praise: extol, laud, lionize, encomium, paean, plaudits. Blame: castigate, excoriate, upbraid, vilify, pillory, opprobrium. Watch the near misses: deprecate (disapprove) is not depreciate (lose value), an aspersion (slur) is not an aspiration (hope), and a eulogy (speech of praise) is not an elegy (mournful poem).

items.ex: The brochure extolled the hotel's views and said nothing about the highway.
Historians laud the treaty as a model of patient diplomacy.

items.a: a speech praising someone, especially one who has died
items.ex: Her granddaughter's eulogy had the whole church laughing and crying at once.

items.a: a formal expression of high praise
items.ex: The retiring judge received encomiums from lawyers she had ruled against.

items.a: a song or speech of joyful praise
items.ex: The documentary is a two-hour paean to the humble bicycle.

items.a: an award or expression of praise
items.ex: The cookbook won every accolade the industry offers.
The rookie's defense earned plaudits even from the rival coach.
Young stars who live on adulation often struggle when it fades.
The town lionized the girl who found the lost hikers.

items.a: the highest point or perfect example of something
d: the lowest point of a decline
items.ex: Fans call the album the apotheosis of 1970s soul.
The plan went ahead with the board's full approbation.
Cutting waste is a laudable goal, but not by closing the library.
The company faced international opprobrium after the spill.
He endured years of obloquy before the records cleared his name.
The report castigated the agency for ignoring the warnings.
Critics excoriated the remake as a lazy cash grab.
The sergeant upbraided the recruit for losing his rifle.

items.a: to warn or reprove firmly but gently
items.ex: The judge admonished the jurors not to read the news coverage.

items.a: to speak of as wicked; to defame
items.ex: Campaign ads vilified the senator as a friend of polluters.

items.a: to speak of as having little worth
items.ex: He disparaged the rival bakery's bread, then quietly bought a loaf.
It is easy to denigrate early aviators whose planes kept crashing.
The editorial deprecated the use of tear gas on peaceful marchers.

items.a: a damaging remark about someone's reputation
items.ex: I cast no aspersions on his honesty; I only question his math.
Critics derided the invention as a toy; it sold ten million units.

items.a: to expose to public ridicule and scorn
items.ex: The tabloids pilloried the minister over a single clumsy remark.
Fans lambasted the team for trading away its best player.

items.a: to call into question the truth or honesty of
items.ex: The defense tried to impugn the witness's memory of the night.
Teachers decried the cuts as a blow to every classroom.
The comment section filled with vituperative posts within the hour.
The champion suffered the ignominy of losing in the first round.

read.title: The Second Novel
text: When Mara Quill's first novel appeared, the reviews read like encomiums. Critics extolled her ear for dialogue, a morning show lionized her as the voice of a generation, and plaudits followed her across a forty-city tour. One magazine called the book the apotheosis of the small-town novel.

Her second book met a colder world. A prominent critic published a vituperative review that went beyond the prose: he impugned her honesty, suggesting she had lifted whole scenes from an obscure older writer. Online, strangers pilloried her, and a few old admirers began to disparage the first book too, as if they had never praised it.

The charge turned out to be false. The older writer herself came forward to decry the accusation, and the critic, admonished by his editor, printed a correction. Quill never sought revenge. Asked years later about the ignominy of that season, she said only that adulation and opprobrium had taught her the same lesson: neither one had really been about her.

q.q: When the critic "impugned her honesty," he
"The ignominy of that season" refers to
o: the honors she won on tour
the public disgrace of the false charge

q.q: In Quill's last remark, adulation and opprobrium are
o: excessive praise and harsh public blame
two stages of drafting a novel
